title: From Adam (1 Chronicles 1)
hookLine: the Tanakh's last book begins with Adam and a list of generations

lines: DIVREI HAYAMIM: THE EVENTS OF THE DAYS.
THE LAST BOOK STARTS AT THE BEGINNING.
cards: Three names, and no introduction. In the King James words, the book begins: "Adam, Sheth, Enosh." No "in the beginning", no setting, no verb.
Just names, generation after generation, chapter after chapter. This is Chronicles, in Hebrew Divrei Hayamim, the words, or the events, of the days.

In the order of books the Talmud lists, it comes last of all, so the Hebrew Bible, which opened with Adam in Genesis, comes back around to Adam at its end. A page of names can look like the part to skip.

teach.b: Chronicles retells the whole story, and it starts by compressing Genesis into lists. Adam to Noah. Noah's sons.
Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, whom the book calls Israel. Then the tribes, one by one, with their families and towns. Why begin like this?
A list of names says quickly what a story can't: nobody here came from nowhere. Every person stands at the end of a long line. And the lists aren't as dry as they look.
Tucked into Judah's family is a man called Jabez. His mother named him that, the text says, because she bore him in pain.

teach.h: JABEZ: A PRAYER IN THE LIST.
teach.b: Then, in the middle of the list, Jabez calls out to God, asking to be blessed and kept from harm, and the text says God granted what he asked.
One small prayer, buried in a genealogy, as if to say every name on this page had a life and a voice.
Now look where the lists end up: at the people who came back from exile and settled again in Jerusalem, people like the ones we've met in Ezra and Nehemiah.

teach.h: FROM ADAM TO THE RETURNED EXILES.
teach.b: So the chain runs from Adam to the returned exiles. One way to read it: the people rebuilding a small city after exile are placed inside a story as wide as humanity. A life can be lived as if it started with itself.
Chronicles opens with a list that says otherwise.

how: Jews read Chronicles as part of the Writings, the third section of the Tanakh; Jewish families also keep track of lineage in ways such as naming children after relatives and recording family names.

o: a claim that only Adam's sons count as Israel
a list of kings who ruled after the exile
a family line traced from the first human to now

s: Chronicles opens with a story of creation
it opens with names: "Adam, Sheth, Enosh."
in the order the Talmud lists, Chronicles is the last book
so the Hebrew Bible begins with Adam in Genesis and returns to him at the end.
the genealogies contain no stories at all
Jabez calls on God in the middle of Judah's list, and God grants his request.

games.q: you're writing the history of a small people rebuilding after exile. where do you start the story?
o: with the building of the Temple.
games.why: Chronicles starts with Adam, and its lists run down through the generations to the people who came home.

practice: Say silently the name of someone who raised you or whose family you come from, a parent, a grandparent, a guardian, an adoptive family, anyone who handed life on to you.
Then go one step further back and say their parent's name; if you don't know it, let the space stand for someone real whose name is simply out of reach, and rest there, at the end of a long line.
If you pray, remember them in words from your tradition.

wordCard.voice: From Adam. Chronicles, last in the Talmud's order of books, opens with Adam and walks the generations down to its own day. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: the Hebrew name of Chronicles, the words or events of the days.

carryVoice: Your line: from Adam to now. Every name on the list had a life and a voice. Day eight hundred eighty-one.
